newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain's top newsagent reports loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain's top newsagent reports loss.

text.p: Britain's leading newsagent, W H Smith Group Plc, on Wednesday reported the first loss in its 204-year history and admitted there were still mountains to climb before peak profits return.
"We've made a good start (to the current year) but we are only in the foothills -- the Himalayas lie ahead," chief executive Bill Cockburn told Reuters.
The company reported a full-year loss of 194.7 million pounds ($303 million) after restructuring charges of around 285 million.

Smiths has undergone a sweeping overhall since Cockburn took charge in January. Since then he has sold off the company's stake in the loss-making Do It All do-it-yourself chain and made more than 1,000 staff redundant.
The changes were seen as vital for the future of the group, which includes the Virgin Our Price music and Waterstones book chains as well as numerous W H Smith outlets.
The group has struggled in recent years with low margins, stores cluttered with too many product lines and increasing competition from supermarkets which have snatched market share.
Cockburn believes the restructuring is already starting to show some signs of bearing fruit, noting that W H Smith outlets had managed to increase market share since the June.

"The books, news, magazines, stationary products are doing quite well," he said. "People who think the supermarkets are taking us to the cleaners is not being borne out in our figures although clearly they do represent a formidable force."

Around 13 million people use the companies' various stores and numbers are slightly up from previous years but Cockburn said the real crunch will come in the run-up to Christmas -- the make or break period for Britain's retailers.
While the outlook for the W H Smith outlets may be optimistic, the picture for Virgin Our Price is cloudy.
"The entertainment product is very disappointing," Cockburn said, blaming slow sales growth on a scarcity of exciting and marketable music, video and computer games.
Fierce competition and sluggish growth in the entertainment business are not the only challenges facing the group.
Cockburn said the redundancies had taken their toll on staff morale but he was hopeful that the worst was now behind it.
"Morale has been a bit thin. Come September the new organisation is in place and then it's all hands to the pump driving for success, particularly with Christmas coming up," he added.
W H Smith shares, which have recently been trading near their year's highest level, were down 4-1/2 pence to 511 as the market remained cautious about the group's prospects.
"We've been a seller of the shares for the past few weeks and we still think they're overvalued," said an analyst at broker Mees Pierson.
